issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a civilian in a war zone, broad self-blame for the event is hard to reconcile unless there are other items indicating a specific morally injurious or preventable action. The rest of the profile centers on external danger cues (being followed/watched, loud sounds, checking safety) and vulnerability, not guilt-linked processing. This appraisal is therefore the main clinically questionable item in the set.

vignette:
Nadia is a 44-year-old married prosecutor who came to treatment after years of trying to keep her life tightly ordered around a sense of danger she no longer felt able to manage. She grew up in the United States in a Middle Eastern family, but as an adult she spent a period of time in a civilian role in a war zone, where the ordinary markers of daily life were repeatedly interrupted by surveillance, sudden noise, and the fear of being singled out. What remains most vivid to her is not a single image so much as the atmosphere of being watched. She remembers moving through streets where voices carried in ways that made her body tense before she even knew why, hearing a man call out in a tone that seemed directed at her and feeling her stomach drop. She remembers the persistent uncertainty of whether someone behind her was merely walking the same route or tracking her movements, and the way that uncertainty could turn an ordinary walk into something acutely perilous. In that setting, the sound of a related voice and the sense of being followed were not abstract fears; they were part of how danger announced itself.

Since returning home, Nadia has built an accomplished professional life, but she describes never having really regained the feeling that the world is basically safe. She has come to believe, with a certainty that feels more like recognition than opinion, that the world is dangerous and that safety exists only in very narrow pockets. Home, with the doors checked and the layout familiar, is one of the few places where she can sometimes settle. Her own office, when the door is shut, can also feel tolerable for short stretches. Beyond that, she experiences much of her day as exposure. At the courthouse she is surrounded by voices, footsteps behind her in corridors, people glancing at her in elevators or through glass partitions, and each of these can sharpen into something loaded. If she hears a voice that resembles the kind of voice that once signaled threat to her, she does not register it as background conversation. Her attention fixes instantly. She turns to locate the speaker, her muscles tightening before she has fully thought it through. Walking from the parking garage to the building, she often checks reflections in windows or the movement of shadows behind her, trying to determine whether someone is simply nearby or whether she is being tracked.

Over time, these habits have narrowed her life. Nadia wakes during the night and checks whether she is safe, listening for signs that something is wrong before trying to sleep again. Unexpected or loud sounds pull her into immediate alertness. A slammed car door outside, raised voices in the street, a sudden bang in the courthouse hallway-each prompts the same quick internal shift, as if her body has decided before she can. She is careful about where she goes and when. She prefers routes, rooms, and routines that give her a sense of control, and she feels markedly less able to cope in places that fall outside those few "safe" zones. She does not describe this as a choice so much as necessity; from her perspective, she is simply being realistic about how exposed the world is.

Nadia is painfully aware of how much this has changed her. She says she used to be a happy person, someone who could laugh easily and absorb the ordinary frustrations of a day without feeling undone by them. Now she experiences herself as persistently miserable, living with a grim expectation that something bad could happen at any time. What frightens her almost as much as the danger itself is her conviction that she can no longer deal with even the slightest upset. A scheduling change at court, an unexpected call, a minor disruption in plans can feel to her like evidence that she is barely holding herself together. At work she still performs at a high level, but it costs her. Colleagues see her as exacting and self-contained; at home her husband has noticed how limited their world has become, how often she declines outings unless she already knows the place and can predict the surroundings.

She sought help after a recent stretch of broken nights and a difficult day at the courthouse when a voice in the corridor stopped her cold and she was suddenly overcome by the certainty that someone was behind her and watching her. Nothing happened, but the episode left her shaken by how small her life had become and how quickly she could be transported into fear in the middle of a workday. Sitting in the intake, she spoke less about wanting to "move on" than about wanting some part of herself back. At the same time, she was wary of treatment, afraid that lowering her guard would be naive in a dangerous world. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to stop caring about safety, but to no longer feel that safety exists only in a few shrinking places.
